at.step: On a million random keys, does finding the median by quickselect take roughly n comparisons, n log n comparisons, or n squared comparisons, in the typical case?

Quickselect partitions around a pivot, exactly as quicksort does, but recurses into only the side that contains the target rank — the other side is discarded outright, never sorted, never visited again. Finding the median of a million random keys this way costs a small constant times n comparisons, against n log n for a full sort of the same keys.

An adversarial or always-unlucky pivot — the first element, on data that is already sorted — degrades quickselect to the same quadratic blow-up unguarded quicksort suffered: each partition shrinks the range by only one element instead of roughly half, so the work adds up like a triangle, not a shrinking geometric sum.

syllabus.clause: deterministic BFPRT with groups of five

at.step: Median-of-medians: split into groups of five, sort each tiny group, take each group's median, then recursively find the median of those group-medians and use that as the pivot. At least three in ten elements are provably smaller than that pivot, and at least three in ten are provably larger — so at most seven in ten survive to the next round, worst case, not merely on average.

The constant hidden inside that worst-case linear bound is large enough — sorting every group of five, two recursive calls every round instead of one — that median-of-medians measurably loses to ordinary randomised quickselect on the same everyday input. A worst-case guarantee, bought at a real and measurable price.
A real standard library promises a worst-case bound for exactly this operation. Does it actually fall back to median-of-medians to deliver that guarantee?

Musser's own 1997 introselect: run quickselect, and only switch to median-of-medians once the recursion depth passes a bound proportional to log n, keeping quickselect's good average case while still guaranteeing linear worst-case time. But reading this machine's own installed standard library header directly shows its actual fallback is a heap-based selection, not median-of-medians at all — the textbook algorithm and the one actually shipped have quietly diverged.
